meta.subtitle: How to use the empty space on wide monitors — options weighed, recommendation, open questions.
meta.summary: Design plan for asymmetric bleed — prose locked, scan-friendly primitives widen to fill the column.

blocks.summary: Today the content column maxes out around 1100px even when the monitor offers 1500+. Prose doesn't benefit from a wider column (readability caps at ~80 chars), but tables, charts, code blocks, and diagrams do. The recommended path is asymmetric bleed: cap prose at the readable column, let scan-friendly primitives extend to the grid-cell edge.
bullets: A — raise --max-width: cheap, breaks prose readability. Rejected as default.
B — asymmetric bleed (prose locked, primitives bleed): recommended.
C — right-rail of supporting content: defer until a concrete second-surface candidate exists.
D — multi-column prose: rejected (awkward in scroll-based reading).

blocks.title: What's there today
blocks.lead: Three width modes selected by the chrome cycler; max-width applies uniformly to every primitive in the content column.

rows: More cards per row; prose still readable.
Whatever the main grid cell gives.

blocks.title: Where the toggle lives
blocks.content: Top-right chrome strip, immediately left of the theme button. The icon is three small boxes — the count of filled boxes reflects the current mode (1 = narrow, 2 = wide, 3 = max). Hover shows the full label ‘Content width: <mode> — click to cycle …’.

blocks.title: Effective ceiling on common viewports
blocks.content: On a 1440px monitor with a 280px sidebar, max mode delivers ~1100px — a tie with wide. On 1920+ monitors max widens past 1500px and prose lines become unreadable. The current cap is silently the wrong cap on either side of that boundary.

blocks.title: The actual problem
blocks.lead: Wide monitors are wasted on prose, valuable for scan-friendly primitives. The current single max-width applies the same rule to both.

cards.title: Prose — narrow wins
items: Past ~80 characters per line, eye saccades farther and re-acquisition slows.
It's a measurable readability limit, not a personal preference.
Every typography-aware platform (Stripe, Notion, Material, GitBook) caps prose at 720–860px regardless of viewport.

cards.title: Scan-friendly primitives — wide wins
items: Tables with many columns benefit from horizontal real-estate.
Code blocks with long lines (URLs, queries, JSON) avoid horizontal scroll.
Charts (scatter / quadrant / multi-series bars) read more accurately at higher width.
Mermaid diagrams with many participants stay legible without overlap.
KPI grids fit more tiles per row, cutting vertical scroll.
Image / live-snippet pairs gain breathing room.

blocks.title: Options
blocks.lead: Five candidates, scored on cost, readability impact, and design surface.

blocks.content: Single-line change. Quick to ship, easy to revert. Wrecks prose readability at 1500+. Not viable as the default.

blocks.title: Rejected
blocks.content: Trades readability for empty-space utilisation. The kit is reader-first; that's the wrong trade.

blocks.title: B — Asymmetric bleed (prose locked, primitives bleed)

blocks.content: Cap prose at ~860px (the readable column). Block-level primitives that are scan-friendly opt-in to wider rendering via a CSS class or per-block attribute, bleeding up to the grid cell.
Two ways to decide which blocks bleed:

, and
at section depth. Narrower primitives (callout, insight, info-tip, list, paragraph, small kpi-grid) keep prose width.

blocks.title: Recommended
blocks.content: Auto-bleed by kind is the right default — readers don't have to know about the option, and the kit's kind set is small enough that the rule lives in one place. Opt-in stays available as an override (rare; explicit when used).

cards.title: What we gain
items: Prose stays readable on every viewport.
Tables / charts / diagrams use the space they actually need.
No new mode for the reader to learn — defaults work.

cards.title: What it costs
items: Centred bleed in a non-sticky main needs the grid-cell width — CSS custom properties + container queries carry it; a JS ResizeObserver is the fallback.
Mixed prose + inline-table sections feel inconsistent at the edges. Pin the rule: bleed at the block boundary, never mid-paragraph.
Existing .hdt-table-wrap.expanded already does an ad-hoc bleed; refactor it to use the same mechanism so there's one bleed system, not two.

blocks.content: Treat the right gutter as a real surface — anchor permanent panels there: section TOC (currently left-side), pinned glossary tooltips, a related-pages rail derived from shared sections, or a notes pad.

cards.title: What we gain
items: All horizontal space is used.
Pinned tooltips no longer overlap the body.
Cross-reference / related-page UX becomes possible.

cards.title: What it costs
items: Substantial layout work. Current grid is left-sidebar + main; needs a third column with breakpoints for narrow → mobile.
Three columns on 1440-class screens squeeze prose toward the centre even when the rail is empty. The rail has to conditionally render.
Each candidate (TOC, pinned tooltips, notes, related links) is its own design decision. We'd settle what lives there before building.

blocks.title: Deferred
blocks.content: Worth doing the day a concrete second-surface candidate justifies the column. Pinned glossary tooltips is the strongest standalone; even then it's a separate design pass.

content: on prose-heavy sections at wide viewports.

blocks.title: Rejected
blocks.content: Awkward in scroll-based reading — readers scroll down for column 1, then up for column 2. Mixes badly with code blocks, tables, charts (must span both columns). No competitor (Stripe, Notion, GitBook, Material) does this.
Render two pages or two sections of one page in parallel columns. Powerful for diffs / before-and-after, niche for most reading.

blocks.title: Deferred
blocks.content: Niche. Adds a navigation mode (which two pages? how to choose them?) and routing complexity for hash-based nav. Revisit if a real use case shows up.

blocks.title: Recommendation
blocks.lead: Ship B with auto-bleed defaults. Collapse the existing three width modes into two. Defer C until concrete. Reject D, defer E.

cards.title: Current (3 modes)
items: narrow — 860px on EVERYTHING (prose + primitives)
wide — 1100px on everything
max — uncapped on everything

cards.title: After B (2 modes)
items: prose-locked — 860px on prose AND primitives (no bleed)
default — prose 860px, primitives bleed to the grid cell

blocks.title: What changes for existing pages
blocks.content: Nothing in source — bleed is auto-applied by kind. Readers who explicitly chose narrow / wide / max in localStorage are migrated: narrow → prose-locked, wide / max → default. The cycler icon stays in the top-right cluster; one click toggles.

blocks.title: Open questions
blocks.lead: Before implementing B, decide each of these — they affect either the data model or the geometry rule.

steps.title: Where the bleed edge sits
steps.content: Out to the grid cell (internally consistent) or out to the viewport minus a fixed gutter (hides the right-edge cue)? Probably grid-cell — keeps the math local to the layout.

steps.title: Annotated-code bleed
steps.content: annotated-code's side panel of annotations needs the prose-width constraint to stay legible. Should the CODE bleed while the panel stays narrow? Likely yes, but the layout needs verifying — the code + panel are siblings today.

steps.title: Kpi-grid threshold
steps.content: 3 tiles fit at 860px; 4 stack to two rows. Should 4-tile grids bleed to a single row, or accept the 2×2? Probably the latter — preserves vertical rhythm.

steps.title: Print stylesheet
steps.content: Bleed shouldn't apply when printing. Add a @media print rule that neutralises .full-bleed margins so the printed page stays inside its sheet.

steps.title: Code-block long-lines composition
steps.content: Bleed solves 'code spans wider than prose,' but readers may also want wrap mode (already per-block). Both compose; document that both exist so authors pick the right tool.

blocks.title: Skip / revisit triggers
blocks.lead: What would cause us to abandon B mid-build or revisit a rejected option.

items: if it ever produces a layout that's 'wide but the eye doesn't know what to land on' — a chart bleeding past the caption it belongs to is worse than tight.
the day a second-surface candidate (pinned tooltip, notes pad, comments) becomes a real concrete spec.
